Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 10 Apr 2027 09:12:00 -07:00
Subject: Burst priming acceptance criteria & follow-up

Hi Danielle —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap from our discovery: QuantaHealth needs sub-200ms p95 for streaming token delivery on your triage assistant, sustained at ~120 concurrent streams during business hours, with spikes to 450 concurrent for short windows (<=6 minutes). You called out two hard constraints: (1) end-user perceived latency under 250ms for SSR flows and (2) deterministic failover to a lower-cost model when capacity is constrained.

Attached is a first-pass "warmup / priming" checklist and a short SLA draft. For clarity, the items we propose to validate during the POC are:
- Warm pool size and priming duration required to hit p95 target at 120 concurrency
- Scale-up time from cold to target concurrency (target: <= 90s to reach 80% capacity)
- Queueing behavior and tail latencies under sustained bursts (6 min windows)
- Streaming token latency and first-byte times under KV cache hits

Proposed next steps:
1) We run a short lab test next week (engineers-only) to collect baseline numbers; Marissa will own test config.
2) QuantaHealth to confirm the safe test window for production-mirroring traffic (suggested: Sun 04/18 03:00-05:00 UTC).
3) Exchange the signed NDA/SLA if legal is comfortable; procurement@quantahealth, please confirm timelines.

Can you confirm the suggested test window and whether procurement needs a redline on the SLA before we run the lab?

—Hannah

Danielle / Hannah —

I pulled together the engine config we recommend for the lab and a short runbook. Key technical points:
- Baseline model: "redwood-1.9b" quantized profile for cost parity; fallback profile: "redwood-1.9b-q2".
- Warm pool priming: we recommend allocating N+20% warm instances where N maps to expected concurrency. For 120 streams we suggest 50 warmed slots (continuous KV cache priming for 10 minutes). This tends to hit p95 targets in our benchmarks.
- Burst ramp: we simulate a step function to 450 concurrent over a 30s injection and hold for 6 minutes; our default queue backend uses a latency-aware token bucket with max queue depth 600; when queue depth exceeds threshold we route to fallback model (configurable).
- Scale-up time target: lab will validate time-to-80% capacity. Our internal median for a similar footprint is ~70s; worst-case observed ~130s depending on backend IO.

I attached the warmup checklist with the exact load generator commands and config settings. For the streaming p95 we will capture: first-byte latency, per-token median, p95, p99 and the number of requests that experienced routing to fallback.

Can procurement sign the SLA redline sample (attached) or do you need a tracked-change version? If procurement wants a DocuSign flow, we can push a prepared DocuSign link after your review.

Thanks —
